name: QC Cannot Replace Classical
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: Why Your Laptop Is Not Getting a Quantum Upgrade
lesson.summary: Even a mature, fully error-corrected quantum computer would not replace classical computers for ordinary tasks, because both the physics of building one and the narrow list of problems it helps with point toward a coprocessor model rather than a wholesale replacement.
lesson.body:
A recurring image in popular coverage of quantum computing is the eventual quantum laptop or quantum phone, an implicit promise that quantum computers are simply a faster next generation of the computers people already use. Given what the previous two chapters established, narrow problem applicability and a failing grade on the general purpose technology tests, it is worth stating plainly why that image is misleading, and doing so from two independent directions: the physics of the hardware and the shape of the problems it solves.

Start with the physical requirements. Useful quantum computation requires qubits to maintain delicate quantum states, superposition and entanglement, that are extraordinarily sensitive to environmental noise. Current leading approaches require cooling hardware to temperatures near absolute zero and isolating it from vibration, electromagnetic interference, and stray heat. On top of that, because individual physical qubits are error prone, achieving one reliable logical qubit under quantum error correction requires combining many physical qubits together, with current estimates running into the hundreds or thousands of physical qubits per logical qubit for the largest problems researchers eventually want to run. None of this is a temporary inconvenience awaiting a clever engineering fix, it follows from how quantum information behaves, and it points toward large, specialized, expensively maintained installations rather than a chip that fits inside a phone.

Now consider the problem side, covered in the previous chapter. Even setting the hardware constraints aside, quantum computers offer no advantage for the overwhelming majority of ordinary computing tasks: browsing a website, editing a document, playing a video, running a database query, or training most machine learning models. For that entire category of work, classical computers are faster, cheaper, and far more energy efficient, with no theoretical reason to expect that to change. Quantum advantage only shows up for the narrow, structured problem types discussed earlier: certain factoring problems, unstructured search, quantum simulation, and some optimization tasks.

Put these two facts together and the realistic architecture that researchers actually describe looks less like a laptop replacement and more like a coprocessor, a specialized accelerator that a classical system calls out to for a specific narrow subroutine, similar in spirit to how a graphics processing unit today accelerates parallel workloads like rendering or deep learning matrix multiplication without replacing the central processor that runs everything else. The classical computer still handles control logic, input and output, storage, and the vast majority of computation. The quantum hardware, likely housed in a specialized facility and accessed remotely, handles only the sliver of work where it has genuine mathematical advantage.

This reframes the right question entirely. The interesting question was never whether quantum computing will replace classical computing, a claim both the physics and the problem set make implausible. The interesting question is smaller and more mundane: for which narrow slice of real-world problems will it be worth the cost and complexity of accessing a quantum coprocessor, and how valuable is that slice likely to be. That is a business and engineering question, not a science fiction one, and it is considerably less exciting than the laptop replacement narrative, which is itself worth noticing.
